title: The Last Keeper's Day-Book
author: Fenna ko-Dreugh, keeper
body:
# Dunnow, the keepers' day-book

*The last pages.*

---

**Thaw, 1023.** Cut the spring's prices on the Kharrow wall: four. A herdsman, a boy drowned at the Bone Ford, a cart of ore, a word said at the Moot that should not have been. Old Haddo says a word is not a debt. I cut it anyway. Everything is a debt if somebody is waiting for it.

**Midsummer.** No prices came up from the Moot. They have a reckoner now at Kharrow, with sticks. Sticks burn.

**Autumn.** Haddo died in his bed in the keepers' rest. I cut him on the blank wall, not in the Tally: he owed nothing and was owed nothing, and it seemed wrong for there to be nowhere he was written.

**Winter.** Cut nothing. Swept the halls. Lit the windows every night so the Windgate would see them.

**Winter, later.** Lit the windows. Nobody came down the Windgate.

**Thaw, 1024.** The Moot has sent a boy to say I am pensioned and may come down. The Tally is to be kept by the Moot from now on, in the reckoner's sticks. I asked the boy who keeps the sticks when the reckoner dies. He did not know.

**The last day.** I have put out the windows. I have left the chisels on the table in case. If anyone reads this who is not a keeper: the Tally is not a list of what people owe. It is a list of who is still owed. They are not the same thing, and the difference is the whole of the law.

*Fenna*

title: The Overman's Book, Winter 1001
author: Brann ko-Brindle, overman at Ghaleld
body:
# Ghaleld, the overman's book

*Winter of 1001.*

---

**First week.** Forty-one hundredweight up the shaft. The deep seam gets redder going down. Old Ilsa says it smells of a forge with nothing in it.

**Second week.** Drove the level past the timbering into the red. The rock is warm. The picks ring longer than they should.

**Third week.** Broke through. I am writing this at the drawing forge with my hands not right. The seam is not a seam. It is grained. It has a hollow in the middle of it the shape of a marrow, and in the hollow the iron is so pure you can draw it cold. And in the hollow there was a thing lying that was the shape of the hollow, and it got up.

**Same night.** We chained it. The last length off our own forge, eight turns round it and the end run into the rock. It stood still for that. I do not know why. Ilsa says it was listening to the iron.

**Fourth week.** Two hundred hundredweight. Two hundred. We cut round it. It watches. Nobody will work the face it can see, so we work behind it.

**Fifth week.** Torvik went to the face it can see. He came back without his pick and would not say.

**Sixth week.** The Moot has heard. Shut by order. The shift goes up tomorrow.

**Same night.** The shift has gone up. I have stayed to bank the forge, which is a lie I will tell the Moot. It is still in its chain. It has not taken its eyes off the drawing forge in six weeks, and I have just understood that it was never looking at us. It was looking at the chain on the hooks. Every length we ever drew, it is the same iron as it is. We have been hanging the heights together with it.

*B.*

title: The Salt Isles Cargo Book
author: kept at the Oskel cave by the Salt Isles masters, in several hands
body:
# Oskel: tides and lading

*The Salt Isles' book for the Oskel lead, kept in the cave, read by every master who put in.*

---

**Rules of the cave.** Come round the north cape on the flood. Lie off till you see the Watch-fire on the cliff, then steer to put the fire on your bow and the gloup's spray on your beam, and you will clear the skerries by a cable. Row in at slack water only. Lie in the pool. The Oskel lower the lead to you down the gloup on their rope, eight pigs a lift. Do not go up the gloup. They do not like it.

**Lading, autumn 1022.** Forty-two lifts. Pigs weighed and marked. Silver in the master's chest, as agreed.

**Lading, spring 1023.** Thirty-eight lifts. The winchman Haldo asks what the silver buys in the Isles. Told him.

**Lading, autumn 1023.** Fifty lifts, the last of the season. The winchman asks when we sail in the spring, and on what tide. Told him.

*(The rest of the book is blank. On the inside of the back board, in a different hand, a line from the north cape to the Watch, and a second line from the cape to a mark below the cliff, and where the second line crosses the skerries, a cross.)*
